claims.text: The patient presented on 2026-01-07 with a severe headache rated 8/10 in intensity, described as sudden onset after exertion, throbbing, diffuse, and associated with mild nausea but no vomiting, visual changes, or radiation.
The patient reported no past medical history, no current medications, and no known allergies.

Social history indicates the patient lives alone, is independent in daily activities, works as a primary school teacher, does not smoke, consumes approximately 6 units of alcohol per week, and engages in regular jogging.
Family history is negative for cerebrovascular accidents, aneurysms, or migraines in immediate family, though the mother has type 2 diabetes and the father has hypertension.

Initial triage and examination on 2026-01-07 recorded a blood pressure of 160/90 mmHg, heart rate of 88 bpm, respiratory rate of 16 breaths/min, temperature of 36.7-36.8°C, and oxygen saturation of 98% on room air.

Initial neurological examinations on 2026-01-07 were unremarkable, showing the patient alert and oriented with no focal neurological deficits, normal cranial nerves, normal motor and sensory function, no neck stiffness, and unremarkable fundoscopy.
A CT head scan performed on 2026-01-07 at 14:45 showed no evidence of intracranial haemorrhage or mass lesion.
Blood tests collected on 2026-01-07 at 15:15 revealed mild leukocytosis (WBC 12.5 x 10^9/L), CRP of 8 mg/L, and normal renal and liver function tests.
On 2026-01-07, the patient was diagnosed with Reversible Cerebral Vasoconstriction Syndrome (RCVS) and admitted to the Neurology ward.
On 2026-01-07, the patient was started on oral nimodipine 60 mg every 4 hours to manage vasospasm.
On 2026-01-07, the patient's blood pressure was 150/92 mmHg, headache was rated 7/10, and blood tests showed mild hypokalemia (K+ 3.3 mmol/L) and marginally elevated CRP (12 mg/L).
On 2026-01-07, the patient was started on oral potassium chloride (KCl) 1 g twice daily to correct hypokalemia.
The patient's GP was contacted on 2026-01-07 at 20:00 to provide an update on admission and the preliminary diagnosis of RCVS.

On 2026-01-08, MRI/MRA confirmed the diagnosis of RCVS, the patient's headache severity reduced to 5/10, blood pressure was 135/85 mmHg, CRP was 12 mg/L, and mild hypokalemia (K+ 3.3 mmol/L) persisted.
On 2026-01-08, the nimodipine dose was adjusted to 30 mg orally every 4 hours, and a repeat MRA was planned for 48 hours later.
On 2026-01-08, the patient received education on RCVS, including the importance of avoiding triggers such as intense physical exertion, stress, and medications like triptans or ergotamines.
On 2026-01-09, the patient's headache severity reduced to 3/10, blood pressure was 125/80 mmHg, and blood tests from the previous day showed mild hyponatremia (sodium 132 mmol/L).
On 2026-01-09, the plan included increasing oral sodium intake through dietary measures and restricting excessive fluid intake to correct hyponatremia, with a repeat MRA planned for 24 hours later.
On 2026-01-09, the rehab team assessed the patient and noted mild residual neck stiffness with no significant functional impairments, deciding to arrange outpatient physiotherapy post-discharge.
On 2026-01-10, the patient's headache severity was 2/10, blood pressure was 125/80 mmHg, and mild hyponatremia (Na 132 mmol/L) was noted on previous tests.
On 2026-01-10, the plan was to maintain nimodipine 30 mg every 4 hours, continue dietary measures for hyponatremia, and perform a repeat MRA on 2026-01-11.
On 2026-01-10, the patient was provided with a discharge planning booklet covering RCVS management, lifestyle modifications, and warning signs, and demonstrated understanding of the information.
On 2026-01-11, the patient's headache severity was 2/10, blood pressure was 125/78 mmHg, and the plan was to continue nimodipine 30 mg every 4 hours and perform a repeat MRA to confirm resolution.
On 2026-01-11 at 10:30, a repeat MRA showed significant improvement in cerebral vasoconstriction, confirming the diagnosis of RCVS, and discharge planning was set for 2026-01-12.
On 2026-01-11, outpatient neurology follow-up was arranged for 4 weeks post-discharge.
On 2026-01-12, the patient reported no further headaches, blood pressure was 130/80 mmHg, and mild hyponatremia (Na 132 mmol/L) was noted.
On 2026-01-12, the patient was discharged with a plan to take nimodipine 30 mg orally four times daily, to be tapered over 2 weeks, and to avoid known triggers.
On 2026-01-12 at 12:00, the patient's GP was contacted to discuss the hospital stay, diagnosis, and discharge medication, which was documented as amlodipine 5 mg once daily.
Medication records conflict regarding the discharge regimen: note-17 documents nimodipine 30 mg four times daily to be tapered over 2 weeks, while note-18 documents amlodipine 5 mg once daily.
